articles.title: Pasig cop apologizes for gun-pointing incident as NAPOLCOM probes case
articles.summary: A police officer in Pasig City on Wednesday apologized after a viral video showed him allegedly pointing a gun at people while intoxicated.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 12:27pm
A police officer in Pasig City on Wednesday apologized after a viral video showed him allegedly pointing a gun at people while intoxicated.
At a press conference, the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) presented the cop identified as Police Staff Sergeant Ryan Rene Balisi.

"Sa aking complainant, humihingi po ako ng tawad. Pasensya na po sa aking maling nagawa. Sana mapatawad mo ako. Sa aking mga kababayan sa buong Pilipinas, sana po ma-ano niyo po ako sa aking mga ginawa ay talaga namang pong inaamin ko pong mali," Balisi said.

(To my complainant, I apologize. I am sorry for what I did wrong. I hope you can forgive me. To my countrymen across the Philippines, I hope you can forgive me for what I did, I truly admit that I was wrong.)
"At sa ating kapulisan, Sir, Ma'am, ako po ay humihingi ng tawad dahil sa mga ginawa ko. Sa mga ibang kapulisan po, huwag niyo po akong tularan na ginawa ko po ito," he added.
(And to our police force, Sir, Ma'am, I apologize for what I did. To other policemen, please don't follow what I did.)
Balisi said he had an argument with his wife before the incident, then decided to follow her when she left their home. He admitted that he lost control of his emotions.
Pasig City Police officer-in-charge Police Colonel Wilson delos Santos said authorities acted promptly after receiving the video and identifying Balisi as the police officer involved.
Police tracked Balisi to his residence and brought him to the station. His firearm was confiscated, and an alcohol breath test was administered.
Balisi had posted bail but remained under restrictive custody upon the order of the regional director. He was also set to be reassigned to the Eastern Police District headquarters.
NAPOLCOM Commissioner Ralph Calinisan said his office would proceed with the administrative complaint filed by the complainant against Balisi.
"May complainant dito sa insidenteng ito laban kay Balisi. So that's why itong complainant na ito, ang siyang naghabla kay Balisi dito sa NAPOLCOM," Calinisan said.
(There is a complainant here in this incident against Balisi. So that's why this complainant is the one who filed the complaint against Balisi here at NAPOLCOM.)
"And we will proceed in handling this complaint. 'Yung complaint most likely will progress to two cases, grave misconduct at saka conduct unbecoming of a police officer," he added.
(And we will proceed in handling this complaint. The complaint most likely will progress to two cases, grave misconduct and conduct unbecoming of a police officer.)
Calinisan pointed out that personal problems and intoxication are not excuses for threatening people with a firearm, adding that such incidents undermine public trust in the police.
Meanwhile, Calinisan said the NAPOLCOM would continue strengthening the screening of police applicants, including comprehensive background investigations and proper neuropsychiatric evaluations.
He also emphasized the need to address the mental health and welfare of serving police officers, noting that the commission had reached out to psychologists and psychometricians for assistance.
Calinisan said police officers experiencing personal difficulties should seek professional help, but reiterated that mental health concerns do not excuse abusive behavior. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Israel election results live: exit polls point to tie between Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs
articles.summary: Both blocs would fall short of the 61 seats needed to form a government as support for Palestinian parties surges

blocks.text: Summary
It’s just after 6am in Tel Aviv where Israelis are waking up to exit polls that show no clear victor in yesterday’s elections, with uncertainty guaranteed at this point.

The polls published by Israel’s major TV networks show Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc tied with the opposition grouping led by Gadi Eisenkot on 51 seats each, short of the 61 seats needed to form a majority coalition government.

Earlier exit polls had Eisenkot winning most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin. Israeli exit polls are often revised after publication and are notoriously imprecise, with the final count often swinging by several seats.

Voter turnout surged to the highest level in more than two decades, underscoring the stakes of an election that has been labelled the most important in the country’s history. More than 77% of eligible voters cast a ballot, according to Israel’s central elections committee, about 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.
Final counting is ongoing, with more than 30% of the votes tabulated so far.

blocks.caption: A supporter of the Likud party waits at an election night rally in Jerusalem. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Palestinian parties are projected to dramatically increase their representation in the Knesset, with predictions they could win as many as 18 seats, up from 10. Experts have said that if Eisenkot falls short of a majority, as the exit polls suggest, he would be obliged to sit down to talk to the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am, to try to form a government – which could take weeks.
It is also possible that Eisenkot could try to govern as a minority government, with informal vote-by-vote agreements that would keep the new coalition afloat.

items: Netanyahu took the stage at a post-election rally in Jerusalem just after 3am, telling his supporters official results will show that “Likud is the largest party in Israel”. He told his supporters that the country must “establish a strong, right-wing national government” – adding that a government that relies on the support of Palestinian parties must not be formed.

Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv that the “Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu’s service as Israel’s prime minister … a worthy leader would have accepted the people’s non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics.” In his speech, he also warned Netanyahu not to “use Israel’s security” for political ends, playing on fears that the prime minister could use this period of uncertainty to launch a new attack on Iran.

The exit polls were released after a last-ditch effort by Netanyahu and several other parties to keep polling stations open beyond their 10pm deadline was rejected by the Central Elections Committee. The prime minister suggested publicly that efforts were being made by the “left and Arabs” to steal the election, a claim rejected by the committee, which said it had seen no evidence of systematic tampering.

articles.title: Marcos says 'don't panic' amid weakening peso
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Wednesday allayed concerns as the Philippine peso hit a new historic low, breaching the P64:$1 level.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 12:04pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Wednesday allayed concerns as the Philippine peso hit a new historic low, breaching the P64:$1 level.
“Well, first of all, do not take it with alarm. Don't panic,” Marcos said in an ambush interview at the Bureau of Corrections in Muntinlupa City.
The President said that his government is trying to defend the peso “as hard as we possibly can.”

“People can take solace in the fact that our policy towards the peso is to continue to defend the peso as hard as we possibly can. We have all the tools to defend the peso. We have all the means to defend the peso,” Marcos said.

“And with that in mind, we will continue to do all that we can to make sure that the value of the peso does not continue to go down, especially relative to the dollar. The dollar is also becoming very strong. But nevertheless, we have the means, as I say,” he added.
The local currency sank to an intraday low of P64.18:$1, weaker than the 33rd record low of P64.17:$1 seen during Tuesday’s closing.
The local unit’s weakness came amid the continuous spike in global crude oil prices due to the Middle East crisis. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Shortly after featuring in the Asian Games, Pokémon UNITE to shut down
articles.summary: Pokémon UNITE will end service in March 2027, just months after featuring in the Asian Games in Nagoya, where the Philippines took home a bronze medal. The Pokémon Company announced on October 27…

blocks.text: Pokémon UNITE will end service in March 2027, just months after featuring in the Asian Games in Nagoya, where the Philippines took home a bronze medal.

The Pokémon Company announced on October 27 that the multiplayer online battle arena game will shut down on March 23, 2027, ending service on both Nintendo Switch and mobile devices. The announcement comes in an unexpected turn for a game that was still part of the regional esports stage at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

The Philippines’ Sibol team secured bronze in Pokémon UNITE after its run ended against Indonesia, adding an Asian Games medal to the country’s esports campaign. The result made the game part of a major international competition shortly before its scheduled closure.

Aeos Gem sales and new UNITE Club memberships have already been suspended, with automatic membership renewals also stopped. Existing members can continue using their benefits until their current membership period ends.

The game will receive a special event and update starting November 12. Players will be able to obtain previously released Unite licenses and Holowear, while a new library feature will let players preserve access to certain records and in-game content after the servers close. Players must download the required library data before the end-of-service date to use the feature afterward.
Competitive play will continue in the meantime. The Pokémon UNITE Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo tournament is still scheduled to take place, with qualifiers beginning December 5, 2026.

For Filipino esports, the announcement puts an unexpected endpoint on a game that recently delivered an international medal. The Philippines’ bronze in Nagoya will remain part of its Asian Games record, even as the game itself heads toward its final months.

articles.title: ‘Backdrop for countless local love stories’: Geelong gingko named Victorian tree of the year
articles.summary:
National trust of Victoria award celebrates much-loved arboreal icons while calling for protection of green spaces

For more than 160 years, a humble ginkgo tree raised from seed in Geelong’s…

blocks.text: For more than 160 years, a humble ginkgo tree raised from seed in Geelong’s botanic gardens has been the backdrop to “countless local love stories”. Standing beneath it is the most popular spot to get married at the park, its branches forming the backdrop of many wedding photos.

Now, in addition to being the largest ginkgo biloba in the state – and possibly Australia – at a whopping 20 metres tall, it has a new claim to fame. The much-adored Geelong icon has been crowned Victoria’s tree of the year.

The National Trust of Australia (Victoria), which runs the awards, announced on Tuesday that Geelong’s ginkgo beat eight other finalists to the 2026 title, receiving 27% of 4,435 public votes cast. Second place went to the smooth bark apple myrtle in Prahran, while Apollo Bay’s myrtle beech was voted third.

To be eligible, trees have to be listed on the National Trust significant tree register, which recognises 2,500 trees in Victoria for their cultural, scientific, and historic value. More than 40 were nominated this year, then narrowed down to nine by a panel of 12 experts and arboriculturists.
The executive manager of gardens and landscapes at the National Trust Victoria, Justin Buckley, said the ginkgo was a “very popular winner”.

blocks.caption: The tree has distinctive stalactite-like growths from its trunk and branches, a feature that only appears on older female gingkos.  Photograph: Daniel Cornell/National Trust Victoria

blocks.text: “It’s a really special tree, and very well loved in that area,” he said.

The ginkgo was planted in 1859, just two decades after the township of Geelong was formally established. The seeds were transported from China, rumoured to have been delivered by a ship’s captain making a stop at Geelong’s port.

Since then, generations of botanic garden workers and volunteers have helped it thrive. Not all have been able to see the unusual stalactite-like growths from its trunk and branches, which only occur in much older female gingko varieties, or enjoy its fruit – which has a reputation for being smelly.

Ginkgos, also known as maidenhairs, are among the most ancient trees on earth, dating back to the Jurassic period more than 160m years ago. In Japan, they’re a symbol of hope, longevity and peace, after six survived the 1945 atomic blast in Hiroshima. They were thought to be extinct in the wild for many centuries before being revived.
Botanic gardens supervisor Sheree Parker said the ginkgo was one of the first trees planted in the park and was also its “most visited and talked about”.
“It’s just starting to awaken now after being dormant,” she said. “We’re really excited.
“It’s our most popular destination to get married as well. We have a lot of weddings on this lawn and a lot of couples like to get married underneath the ginkgo.”
The city of greater Geelong staff had been strongly lobbying for the ginkgo to be crowned since the finalists were announced, posting regularly to social media encouraging people to vote.
“As … the backdrop for countless local love stories, she holds a special place in all our hearts,” they said a post earlier this month.
The competition was established in 2016 to celebrate Victoria’s best-loved trees, while also calling for greater protection of green spaces.

A recent urban greening framework, released by Stonnington city council, found over the past decade, more than 17.9 hectares of tree canopy had been lost on private lands in the inner Melbourne suburb alone.

The National Trust is urging the Victorian government to give automatic statutory protection to trees on its register and those of local councils, while also introducing a “retain first” planning principle making tree removal a genuine last resort.

In the past year, the Victorian government introduced uniform protection of canopy trees, but Buckley said it remained “quite limited” and there was “large scope” for significant trees to be removed without a permit.

“The reason we continue to draw attention to trees through this competition is because they really don’t have adequate protection, certainly not the same protection that heritage buildings have,” Buckley said.
“You can’t just think, well, we’ll take this one out, we’ll put another tree in there and everything will be fine. Big significant trees are virtually irreplaceable.
“As we need to accommodate growing populations and more housing … there’s going to be a lot of pressure on trees.”

articles.title: Ex-Sara Duterte aide Jefry Tupas accuses NBI of harassment over recommendation of charges
articles.summary: Former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas on Wednesday accused the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) of harassment.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 10:40am
Former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas on Wednesday accused the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) of harassment.
This was after the bureau recommended the filing of charges against Tupas before the Department of Justice (DOJ).
“I denounce the NBI’s recommendation to file charges against me before the Department of Justice (DOJ). This is harassment, plain and simple,” he said.
“The NBI can file all the trumped-up charges they want against me, but I will never allow myself to be used as a witness for a case built on lies,” he added.
GMA News Online has reached out to the NBI for comment, but it has yet to reply as of posting time.
The NBI earlier filed a referral with the DOJ against Tupas for cyberlibel, obstruction of justice, and publication of false news.
This stemmed from the sworn statement submitted by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Gracioso claimed that he delivered cash to Vice President Sara Duterte, former President Rodrigo Duterte, and Davao Representative Paolo Duterte on the instructions of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
He also claimed that Tupas received the cash on behalf of the Vice President.
Tupas has denied Gracioso’s claims and submitted his affidavit with the bureau.
Sara Duterte, Paolo Duterte, and Velasco have submitted affidavits denying the allegations against them.
'Deceptive maneuvers'
Tupas, meanwhile, alleged that NBI agents offered him cash and a place to stay in the upscale Forbes Park in Makati City.

In his new statement, Tupas questioned the NBI investigation saying he had presented evidence to disprove allegations made by Gracioso including airline ticket bookings, passport photos bearing stamps, and Facebook posts.

Tupas disputed NBI chief Melvin Matibag's statement that he was the source of information about threats to his security. According to Tupas, NBI agents, led by Special Assistant for Mindanao Concerns Voltaire Rovira, were the ones who went to his home in North Cotabato on the morning of September 29.
He noted that he did not ask the NBI to issue a subpoena.
According to him, he requested a formal invitation from Matibag during a telephone conversation regarding the NBI's offer to place him under protective custody.
“Imbes na invitation letter, ang ibinigay ng NBI noong hapon ng September 29, 2026 ay isang subpoena na may petsang September 28, 2026—isang araw bago pa man sila dumating sa aming bahay,” he said.
(Instead of an invitation letter, what the NBI gave on the afternoon of September 29, 2026 was a subpoena dated September 28, 2026—a day before they even arrived at our house.)
He questioned the agency's motives.

“Now that he has publicly identified me as a witness, the apprehension over Matibag’s invitation for a meeting in Manila and the offer for a protective custody becomes completely justified,” Tupas said.
“It is now glaringly obvious that these were not genuine gestures for my safety, but rather deceptive maneuvers to trap me and force me into becoming a false witness,” he added.
Tupas alleged that he was being harassed and pressured to testify against the Vice President in a plunder case linked to Gracioso's allegations.

“It is clear to me, and probably to everyone else who can read between the lines, that I am being harassed, intimidated, and pressured to turn against Vice President Sara Duterte and testify against her in a plunder case related to the Gracioso allegations (as shown in the September 28, 2026 subpoena delivered to my house),” he said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: US costs of Iran war rise to over $47B – Pentagon data
articles.summary: The Pentagon's latest estimate is tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict

blocks.text: PENTAGON. The Pentagon building is seen in Arlington, Virginia, US, October 9, 2020.
Carlos Barria/REUTERS
The Pentagon's latest estimate is tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict

items: The US military has spent over $47 billion on the war in Iran, exceeding previous estimates by more than 25%.
The rising costs of the war are impacting Republican candidates' support ahead of the upcoming elections, as well as President Trump's approval ratings.
The Pentagon's latest estimates include significant costs for replacing munitions and military equipment, with plans for potential escalation in combat operations after the midterm elections.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.

The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.

The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.
More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “platform losses,” which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.
Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting ​that the conflict would last a short time.

Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful.
But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.

Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.
The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth‘s July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war.

While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks. Rappler.com

articles.title: ICC victims ask Chamber to admit witness testimony vs Rodrigo Duterte
articles.summary: The Common Legal Representatives of Victims (CLRV) has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to grant the Prosecution"s request to admit the previously recorded testimonies…

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 9:50am

The Common Legal Representatives of Victims (CLRV) has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to grant the Prosecution’s request to admit the previously recorded testimonies of three witnesses in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte.
In an eight-page document dated October 27, the CLRV said the testimonies do not appear to concern the acts of Duterte.
It said the testimonies appear relevant and corroborative to the accounts of other witnesses and relate primarily to the contextual elements of crimes against humanity.

“Furthermore, the CLRV supports the Request on the ground that the introduction of the prior recorded testimonies and related documents would be consistent with the victims’ rights to a fair and expeditious trial, and [REDACTED], [REDACTED],” it said.
According to the CLRV, the testimonies concern the alleged extrajudicial killings in Central Luzon and fall within the scope of Count 3.

“The prior recorded testimonies and related documents appear to have sufficient indicia of reliability, having been voluntarily recorded during the Prosecution’s investigation in the Philippines,” it said.
“Their introduction would also serve the interests of justice by contributing to the expeditious conduct of the proceedings and conserving the Court’s time and resources,” it added.
The document was signed by lawyers Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan, and Paolina Massida.
Duterte is facing charges of crimes against humanity in connection with the alleged extrajudicial killings in the war on drugs during his term as president and during his term as mayor of Davao City.
He was arrested in March 2025 at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3 and is currently detained at the ICC Detention Center in Scheveningen in The Hague, the Netherlands.
Duterte's trial will start on November 30.
The ICC Trial Chamber III found Duterte fit to stand trial, stating that he “is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings.” —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: SC: Employees cannot be forced to retire before age 65 without consent
articles.summary: In the case, the SC finds Colegio de San Juan de Letran in Laguna guilty of illegal dismissal

blocks.text: EMPLOYEES. A number of senior citizens participate in a pre-screening and orientation on March 18, 2026, at the Department of Manpower Development and Placement (DMDP) office in Cebu City for employment opportunities available to those aged 60 to 65 who are still willing and able to work.
Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler
In the case, the SC finds Colegio de San Juan de Letran in Laguna guilty of illegal dismissal

items: The Supreme Court ruled that employers cannot force employees to retire early without their consent, affirming that the mandatory retirement age is 65.
In the case of Rodolfo Ondevilla, the Court found Colegio de San Juan de Letran guilty of illegal dismissal as there was no mutual agreement for his early retirement.
The ruling awarded Ondevilla full back wages, separation pay, and retirement benefits, emphasizing that his retirement was involuntary and treated as illegal dismissal.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that employers cannot force their employees to retire early without an agreement.

In a decision penned by Associate Justice Ramon Paul Hernando, and was made public on Tuesday, October 27, the SC 1st Division said employees cannot be made to retire from their position before the mandatory retirement age of 65 without their clear and voluntary consent.
Hernando, in the case, partly granted the petition of Rodolfo Ondevilla and found Colegio de San Juan de Letran (CSJL) in Laguna guilty of illegal dismissal.
Ondevilla asserted in his SC petition that he never agreed to retire before 65. The SC accepted his position.

Hernando explained that under the country’s Labor Code, the retirement age is set by an existing agreement or employment contract. If there’s no agreement or contract, then the mandatory retirement age of 65 will be applied, along with the minimum age for optional retirement of 60.

The ruling explained that optional retirement is based on a voluntary agreement between the employer and employee, and the latter must freely agree to it without pressure or coercion. But the SC said in the Ondevilla case that the early retirement happened despite the lack of a mutual agreement between the parties.

Based on the decision, the SC said CSJL never made any proposal for a retirement plan to the petitioner that he could accept or reject, adding that there was no indication that the school was willing to discuss Ondevilla’s retirement.

The High Court added Ondevilla’s objection to his supposed early retirement, along with his illegal dismissal complaint, showed that he had no intention of availing himself of optional retirement before reaching the age of 65.
“Because his retirement was involuntary, the SC treated it as an illegal dismissal. Ondevilla was therefore entitled to full back wages and separation pay instead of reinstatement,” said the ruling.

The SC also awarded him retirement benefits covering his employment from June 16, 2004, until August 29, 2024, when he reached the mandatory retirement age of 65. It directed the arbitration branch to compute the total amount due to him.
Ondevilla started working for CSJL as a comptroller in 2004, and later worked as assistant vice president for finance. He was renewed for work several times.

When the school had a management reorganization in 2018, he was reassigned as controller. Although he objected to this and said it was a demotion, he continued working with the same salary and employee benefits.
CJSL considered Ondevilla’s appointment expired on August 29, 2019, when he turned 60.
The petitioner then filed a complaint for illegal dismissal. He secured victories from the Labor Arbiter, and then from the National Labor Relations Commission.
The case reached the Court of Appeals (CA). It found that Ondevilla had been illegally dismissed, but ruled that a letter he sent to the school showed that he had agreed to retire on July 31, 2020.
When he filed the petition with the SC, Ondevilla challenged the CA’s findings and argued that he never agreed to retire early. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump says government to ‘terminate’ Biden-era methane emissions rules
articles.summary:
Critics warn of climate danger as president in Texas claims change will save companies and consumers billions

Donald Trump announced his administration is “terminating” Biden-era regulations…

blocks.text: Donald Trump announced his administration is “terminating” Biden-era regulations holding oil and gas companies accountable for large leaks of planet-warming methane during a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday evening.

Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save consumers and energy producers $45bn and unlock 210 million barrels of oil – equivalent to about 10 days of US petroleum consumption. “Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators.
The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices stemming from the US war in Iran.

In a press release, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, Lee Zeldin, praised what he called Trump’s move “to end the war on oil and natural gas” by revising oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act.

According to the EPA, the proposal is expected to save $45bn in costs to consumers and businesses, including small businesses operating marginal wells, and produce an estimated 210m additional barrels of oil and 1.41tn cubic ft of natural gas.

Although some oil and gas executives spoke publicly in favor of the landmark methane rule, industry trade groups and corporations worked behind the scenes to gut the methane regulations, according to trade association materials and records obtained via the Freedom of Information Act by Fieldnotes, an oil and gas watchdog organization.
The 2024 methane rule required oil and gas operators to eliminate and minimize leaking, flaring and venting of methane and of volatile organic compounds, which are harmful to human health.

It was the first time the federal government had set nationwide requirements to limit methane emissions from existing oil and gas facilities. An earlier rule finalized under the Obama administration in 2016 applied to new and modified sources. Under the rule’s super emitter program, companies had to investigate major leaks near oil and gas facilities detected by third parties using EPA-approved remote sensing technology.

In March 2025, EPA administrator Lee Zeldin announced that the agency was reconsidering the Biden-Harris regulations “to ensure that they do not prevent America from unleashing energy dominance and continuing our trajectory as a leader in clean energy and emissions reductions”.
Last year, the US emitted more methane from its oil and gas sector than any other country in the world. Methane is responsible for at least a quarter of today’s warming.

Julia Kane, a researcher for Fieldnotes, said the Trump Environmental Protection Agency was giving oil and gas corporations exactly what they want. “The oil and gas industry says it’s a ‘good-faith’ partner eager to help craft regulations, but time and time again it’s worked behind the scenes to delay and weaken them,” she said.

Records obtained by Fieldnotes, including calendar events, presentation slides and meeting request forms, show that industry groups and companies met with the EPA to discuss methane regulations at least 38 times during the current administration’s first year.

“I do think it’s just an extraordinary level of access,” Kane said, adding that industry groups themselves were pleasantly surprised by their access under Trump. For example, during a conference call with industry representatives last year, Independent Petroleum Association of America executive Lee Fuller described a discussion with EPA staff, saying: “It was one of the more fascinating meetings that we’ve ever had, just because they were suddenly willing to talk to us. And they were also suddenly willing to talk about things that we’ve been trying to get them to do for years, and they’ve never even let it come on to the radar screen.”

At a Trump rally in Corpus Christi earlier today, Trump shouted out Harold Hamm, saying the founder of Continental Resources was in the audience. In April, Continental Resources wrote a letter to the EPA pushing back against measures in the methane rule that prohibit routine flaring of associated gas.

Since the EPA announced it would no longer enforce oil and gas regulations in March 2025, oil and gas operators have leaked, vented or flared $7bn worth of natural gas, according to calculations by the Environmental Defense Fund.

Rosalie Winn, senior director and lead counsel at the Environmental Defense Fund, said the Trump administration was seeking to curtail the federal government’s ability to do anything to address climate pollution across all of the largest sectors responsible for emissions.
“What this administration is doing is enabling the worst polluters in the industry to continue to make ever more money off the back of American consumers while they’re wasting energy,” she said.
Robert Mackey contributed reporting

articles.title: Criminal case against alleged Bondi terrorist delayed amid ‘unprecedented’ investigation
articles.summary:
Naveed Akram, 24, has been charged with 78 offences after allegedly committing a terrorist act. The case has been adjourned until February

  • Follow our

blocks.text: The criminal case against Naveed Akram for his alleged role in the Bondi terror attack faces more delays after an “unprecedented” investigation by the joint counter-terrorism team.

The matter will not return to court until 24 February after it was adjourned on Wednesday before Sydney’s Downing Centre local court. Prosecutors expect to be ready to certify the charges against Akram, who is yet to enter a plea, by that date.
Akram, 24, and his father, 50-year-old Sajid Akram, allegedly murdered 15 people after opening fire at a Hanukah festival at Bondi beach on 14 December. Forty people were injured.

Naveed Akram, who survived a shootout with police, has been charged with 78 offences, including 15 counts of murder and one count of committing a terrorist act that investigators allege may have been “inspired by Isis”. Sajid Akram was shot and killed by police at the scene.
Akram was charged with 59 offences in December, with 19 more added in April as the investigation progressed.

The prosecutor, Danielle New, made the application for the adjournment, without opposition from Akram’s defence team, on Wednesday. She said prosecutors had now completed their brief of evidence, which had also been beset by delays due to the sheer volume of evidence involved in the case.

The judge, Karen Stafford, granted the adjournment after New argued more time was needed so investigators could consult the Akrams’ alleged victims and next of kin on the charges laid against Akram ahead of the offences being certified before the court.
This certification process is a standard step in a criminal case, whereby prosecutors formally list the offences proceeding to trial.
New said her team did not want to “rush” the consultations and were conscious that Hanukah was approaching, as well as the Christmas holidays and summer shutdown period for the courts.
“It’s important the crown goes over everything again, to make sure no person’s narrative is left untold,” New told the court.
after newsletter promotion

New said the brief of evidence included thousands of witness statements, medical records, financial statements and purchases made by the Akrams, and footage from Bondi beach on the evening of the attack.

“The [joint counter-terrorism team] has engaged in an investigation the size of which has been unprecedented,” New told the court. “The commitment by all involved is nothing short of highly professional.”

In December, the police “fact sheet” – which was released via the courts and outlined the then allegations against Naveed Akram – alleged there was evidence that the pair “meticulously planned this terrorist attack for many months”. This allegedly included the creation of an “ISIS inspired” video, firearm training and the making of explosives.

The pair, police said in the document, allegedly undertook a “reconnaissance” visit to Bondi two days before the attack, visiting the footbridge from which they are accused of deliberately firing at those gathered at the Jewish festival.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] One peso, two fortunes: The hidden energy bill
articles.summary: The Philippines' underlying vulnerability is a structural imbalance between the dollars the country earns and those it spends

blocks.text: The Philippines' underlying vulnerability is a structural imbalance between the dollars the country earns and those it spends

items: The depreciation of the peso creates a disparity in purchasing power between overseas Filipino workers and domestic wage earners, with the former benefiting from increased remittances while the latter face rising costs.

The Philippines' heavy reliance on imported energy exacerbates the economic strain, leading to a projected $19.1 billion current-account deficit and significant capital flight, which further weakens the peso.

To achieve a sustainable recovery, the country must reduce its dependence on imported energy and enhance its export earning capacity, as temporary gains for some may be offset by higher costs for others.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

When a household opens a higher electricity bill, it is also confronting a currency problem. The peso’s slide creates a stark divide across the country: extra cash for families receiving dollars, but steeper costs for those earning pesos. Yet even that apparent windfall carries an invisible tax. Because the Philippines relies heavily on imported energy, currency depreciation and global commodity swings compound, draining household budgets, raising operational overhead, and eroding the foreign exchange reserves the broader economy requires to keep operating.

For Elena, a nurse in California, the peso’s decline looks like a modest salary increase. Sending $1,000 to her mother yielded P60,000 at a P60 exchange rate; at P64, it yields P64,000 before transfer fees.

But for Ramon, a delivery driver paid strictly in pesos, that same currency movement brings costlier pump prices and fewer groceries. Neither has changed jobs, worked longer hours, or shifted productivity, yet their purchasing power moves in opposite directions.

Their lived experiences capture the uneven consequences of currency depreciation. Overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) and their dependents appreciate the extra cash, while domestic wage earners absorb the pain of rising prices.
Even Elena’s mother cannot treat the extra P4,000 as pure windfall. A good portion will simply cover goods and services made pricier by the weaker peso—starting with her power and grocery bills.

On October 27, the peso closed at P64.17 per dollar, extending its slide despite an unexpectedly sharp 50-basis-point policy rate hike to 5.50% by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) the previous week.

blocks.caption: Philippine peso sinks to record low P64.17 vs $1 | The wRap

blocks.text: The currency’s brief bounce quickly faded, exposing the limits of monetary defense when an economy must continually spend massive amounts of foreign exchange on basic necessities.

The underlying vulnerability is a structural imbalance between the dollars the country earns and those it spends. The BSP projects a $19.1-billion current-account deficit this year, equivalent to 3.8% of gross domestic product.

Capital flight compounds this strain: BSP figures for January through August show net foreign portfolio investments recording $4.254 billion in net outflows, reversing $4.583 billion in net inflows a year earlier. That nearly $8.84-billion adverse swing explains why dependable remittance receipts have failed to halt depreciation. (READ: Martin Romualdez’s properties: Where and how much?)

Energy sits squarely at the center of this dollar drain. Building a gas-fired power station on domestic soil does not transform imported fuel into a local resource. World Bank trade data show Philippine liquefied natural gas (LNG) import spending jumped 52.6%—from $767.73 million in 2024 to $1.171 billion in 2025.

Over the same period, imported physical volumes rose 41.7% to roughly 1.68 million tons. Notably, roughly 79% of that $403.62-million increase came from buying more physical fuel, with higher unit values accounting for the rest. This demonstrates how expanding reliance swells the external bill long before an exceptional global price shock hits.

In the broader trade account, Philippine Statistics Authority data reveal that imports of mineral fuels, lubricants, and related materials grew by $2.56 billion in the first half of 2026, accounting for 21% of total import growth and equivalent to 37% of the widening merchandise trade deficit.

By comparison, August figures show fuel imports reached $1.85 billion, while electronics imports of $4.51 billion were more than offset by $6.20 billion in exports. Electronics generates net foreign exchange; imported fuels represent an unhedged dollar drain.

At the generation level, the arithmetic is unforgiving. Consider an illustrative facility requiring seven million British thermal units of fuel to generate one megawatt-hour. At $10 per unit and an exchange rate of P58, fuel costs alone amount to P4.06 per kilowatt-hour.

If international fuel jumps to $30 and the exchange rate weakens to P63, that fuel component surges to P13.23 per kilowatt-hour before factoring in other generation costs. While actual tariff recovery depends on power contracts and regulatory treatment, consumers ultimately face a bill that incorporates both the global commodity spike and the currency depreciation that magnifies it.

This dynamic ripples across corporate ledgers and family tables alike. Consider Miguel, who runs a business process outsourcing firm billed in dollars while paying salaries and rent in pesos. Depreciation widens his operating margin, provided clients do not demand price cuts and domestic overhead remains manageable. Freelancers with foreign clients share that advantage. (READ: [Vantage Point] Gig Economy: Growth engine or precarious lifeline?)

Across town, bakery owner Liza faces the painful reverse. Her walk-in customers pay in pesos, but imported flour, packaging, and commercial electric utility bills expose her directly to dollar costs. She must decide whether to raise bread prices and risk customer resistance, or absorb the cost hikes and watch her livelihood shrink. Airlines, import-heavy manufacturers, and firms servicing unhedged dollar debt confront identical pressures. Their resilience depends on pricing power, hedging strategies, and whether they generate dollar revenue.

Gas power undeniably provides controllable electricity when other plants falter, and system outages carry severe economic costs. Clean alternatives like solar, wind, and battery storage demand substantial upfront capital, grid expansion, and adequate storage duration.

Yet dependable supply must remain affordable under adverse economic conditions. Energy planners must disclose what proposed capacity actually costs when fuel prices spike and the peso tumbles, identifying who truly bears the foreign-exchange risk.

A lasting recovery demands firmer foundations: stable foreign investment, greater export earning power, and genuine relief from expensive imported energy. Elena may welcome the extra pesos, and Miguel may enjoy healthier margins. But Ramon and Liza have good reason to worry.

The decisive policy test is whether the country can break its avoidable dependence on imported energy before the temporary gains enjoyed by some are completely swallowed by the higher bills imposed on everyone else. – Rappler.com

articles.title: WATCH: US War chief Hegseth arrives in PH for ASEAN defense meeting
articles.summary: United States Secretary of War Pete Hegseth arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday night to attend the ASEAN Defense Ministers" Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus).

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 9:05am
United States Secretary of War Pete Hegseth arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday night to attend the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus).
The US Department of War shared a video of Hegseth’s arrival on its official Facebook page.
The Philippines is hosting the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) and the 13th ADMM-Plus on October 28 and 29 in Cebu.
ADMM-Plus brings together ASEAN defense ministers and their counterparts from dialogue partner countries to discuss regional security issues and strengthen defense cooperation.
This year’s theme is “Navigating Our Future Together.”
ADMM is ASEAN's highest defense consultative and cooperative mechanism, according to the Department of National Defense (DND).
The ADMM-Plus expands defense cooperation to eight dialogue partners including Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States.
The South China Sea and the West Philippine Sea are expected to be among the topics discussed during the meetings.

Other anticipated areas of cooperation include maritime security, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, counterterrorism, peacekeeping operations, military medicine, humanitarian mine action, and cybersecurity.

Manila’s broad priorities in its bilateral relations with the US include strengthening the alliance, defense modernization, and future capacity and capability building, according to the DND. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘I use disposable cups’: Chris Minns backflips on takeaway coffee cups after media and business backlash
articles.summary:
Legislation requiring mugs to be offered when people drink at cafes, to be scrapped with environment minister stating ‘we need to clear this up’

  • Follow our

blocks.text: The New South Wales government has backflipped on its plan to force cafes to offer customers who dine in the option of mugs and glasses instead of takeaway cups.
The Chris Minns government will also ditch a law that would have required businesses to participate in a reusable cup scheme or risk a fine up to $110,000.
Labor reversed its position a week after the legislation passed parliament, following a backlash from small businesses and News Corp Australia.
The reform was part of the Minns government’s plan to reduce plastic waste given Sydney’s landfill is projected to run out by 2030.
The laws to be axed would have made it a requirement for cafes to offer mugs or glasses when customers dined in from 2028.
The NSW environment minister, Penny Sharpe, told 2GB radio on Wednesday morning that the government would repeal the laws relating to mugs and glasses and the potential $110,000 fine.
“We know small businesses are under pressure and we want them to be able to operate in the way that they need to operate, to run their business,” she said.
“It was always the plan that there would be extensive exemptions.”

Separate reforms requiring businesses to accept customers’ own reusable cups – so long as they are “clean” – will remain in place. So too will a law requiring single-use takeaway cups to be recyclable by 2028.

The Daily Telegraph ran a front page last week with the headline “‘Nup’ to the Cup”. There were multiple stories with small business owners criticising the cost of participating in the reusable cup scheme.
The premier, Chris Minns, had defended the legislation in an interview on 2GB on Tuesday, stating the government was “not getting rid of disposable cups anywhere in any place”.
“I use disposable cups, most people use disposable cups,” he said. “I don’t know whether we’ve done a good enough job of explaining the policy.”
On Wednesday, Sharpe said she had spoken with Minns.
“We said: ‘Look, do we need to mandate this?’ Sharpe said. “No, we don’t, and that’s why it’s really important that we need to clear this up.”

blocks.caption: The legislation won’t be repealed until after the March 2027 election Photograph: Boonchai Wedmakawand/Getty Images

blocks.text: Sharpe has asked the NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA) to issue a “statement of regulatory intent” to make clear the government was not progressing with certain changes.
The legislation won’t be repealed until after the March 2027 election. Only two sitting weeks remain before parliament is dissolved.
On Tuesday, the NSW opposition had said if elected next year it would repeal the laws which it claimed “add another layer of regulation that is suffocating NSW businesses”.
Labor is under pressure from the Coalition and One Nation. Both are running pro-small business platforms and pledging significant cuts to payroll tax.
One Nation has said it would cut the tax employers pay on wages by half, slashing it completely in regional areas.
Last week, Minns backed down from implementing changes to several local and regional rail line timetables following a backlash from commuters.
A Guardian Essential conducted last week suggested Labor and One Nation were neck and neck on 28% of the primary vote nationwide with the Coalition on 23%.
Minns told 2GB on Tuesday that “by any poll, by any measure”, NSW’s One Nation leader, Mike Newman, would be premier or opposition leader following the March poll.
The premier has called on One Nation to cost its election policies through the NSW budget office but Newman has refused to commit the party to this.

articles.title: Australia’s inflation rate rises to 4.3%, fuelling fears of fifth interest rate hike this year
articles.summary:
CPI release comes ahead of Reserve Bank decision next week as the Middle East conflict intensifies the cost of living crisis

Australia’s headline inflation rate has accelerated to 4.3%, with…

blocks.text: Australia’s headline inflation rate has accelerated to 4.3%, with a key gauge that strips out volatile prices also elevated, sharpening expectations of another interest rate rise next week.
The Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred measure of consumer prices, called underlying inflation, came in at an annual 3.6% to September.
RBA officials have strongly indicated the board may need to lift borrowing costs further to drag price growth back toward its 2.5% target, citing concerns of a “materially worse” inflation outlook.
The CPI release comes shortly ahead of the central bank’s next monetary policy decision on 3 November, when most economists are tipping another cash rate increase.
The official rate, which informs lending rates including mortgages, already stands at 4.6%, its highest level in 15 years.

CPI figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday show that costs for everyday goods and services are rising at the same time as unemployment lifts, making life uncomfortable for households.
The dynamic also feeds into the growing political unease in Australia and elsewhere, as voters express their discontent with cost of living pressures.

articles.title: Chinese ships seen near Bajo de Masinloc amid fuel aid mission for Filipino fishers
articles.summary: Chinese Coast Guard and People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) ships were seen near Bajo de Masinloc during a Philippine government mission to deliver fuel assistance to Filipino fishermen on Tuesday,…

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 8:36am

Chinese Coast Guard and People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) ships were seen near Bajo de Masinloc during a Philippine government mission to deliver fuel assistance to Filipino fishermen on Tuesday, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said Wednesday.
In a statement, PCG spokesperson for West Philippine Sea (WPS) Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said a Chinese research vessel operating near the shoal was also seen.
“The mission was completed without any untoward incident,” Tarriela said.

The Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) led the mission under the Kadiwa ng Bagong Bayaning Mangingisda (KBBM) Program. The program provides fuel and ice to Filipino fishermen and purchases their fresh catch directly at sea to help lower operational costs and sustain their presence in the WPS.

The mission was carried out by BFAR vessel MV Mamalakaya, with support from PCG vessel BRP Malapascua (MRRV-4403) and PCG Islander 251 aircraft, which conducted a maritime domain awareness flight to ensure the safety of the fishermen and the BFAR vessel.
PCG Commandant Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan directed the deployment of the Coast Guard's sea and air assets to secure the mission.

blocks.caption: Photo from PCG

blocks.text: Photo from PCG
Upon the arrival of MV Mamalakaya, around 40 to 50 Filipino fishing boats operating in the traditional fishing ground approached the vessel and lined up to receive fuel assistance.
Bajo de Masinloc is located 124 nautical miles off Masinloc, Zambales, and is considered within the Philippines' 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago including Luzon Sea and the waters around, within and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —VAL, GMA News

articles.summary: Intensifying hostilities between Yemen and Saudi Arabia further disrupt oil supplies and heighten the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the Iran war began

blocks.text: HOUTHI FIGHTERS. Newly recruited Houthi fighters stand during a rally to commemorate the late leader of Lebanon's Hezbollah, Hassan Nasrallah, and to show support to Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, in Sanaa, Yemen, on October 4, 2024.
Khaled Abdullah/Reuters
Intensifying hostilities between Yemen and Saudi Arabia further disrupt oil supplies and heighten the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the Iran war began

items: The Houthis claimed to have attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery with a ballistic missile, escalating tensions in the region.
The attacks included strikes on Saudi military aircraft and an airbase, while Saudi authorities reported intercepting two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh.
The ongoing conflict has disrupted oil supplies and undermined a previous UN-brokered truce, with regional powers seeking to reduce tensions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
DUBAI, UAE – Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday, October 27, they had hit Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura oil refinery, the ⁠biggest in the kingdom, with a ballistic missile.
Intensifying hostilities between Yemen and Saudi Arabia have further disrupted oil supplies and heightened the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the Iran war began.
The Houthis also said they had attacked Saudi military aircraft and repelled an advance by Saudi-backed forces near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important Red Sea shipping route.

The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the strike on the Ras Tanura refinery had caused a fire at the complex, which also includes a shipping terminal and is located on the Gulf, west of the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike.
Ras Tanura, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, was shut for a period in the early months of the Iran war as a precautionary measure.
Nearly all Saudi Arabia’s oil exports flow through two main ports: Ras Tanura in the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea, both of which the Houthis have attacked in the past.
Bloomberg News cited a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura’s terminal.

The ​Houthis said they had attacked two military transport jets at Najran Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. They also said they attacked the Saudi defense ministry building in Riyadh, and Abha airport.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the attacks.
On Tuesday afternoon, civil defense authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Falling debris from the interception of two ballistic missiles over Riyadh caused material damage to a building, a construction site and a vehicle, the Saudi Civil Defense said later on Tuesday.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh.
The Houthis said they had repelled an advance by forces they described as Saudi-backed from the southern approaches to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces earlier this month pushed the Houthis out of coastal areas they had seized in September, loosening the group’s grip on a vital Red Sea oil route.
Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported Saudi strikes on the Yemeni city of Mocha. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.
The fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce between the coalition and the Houthis, who control the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
On Monday, October 26, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran to try to reduce regional tensions.
Parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the three countries in a mutual defense pact, authorized Egypt’s military on Monday to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Danny Masterson loses appeal against rape conviction after arguing judge was biased against Scientology
articles.summary:
That ’70s Show actor was sentenced to 30 years in prison for two counts of rape against two women, who were also Scientologists

Danny Masterson has lost the appeal of his rape conviction,…

blocks.text: Danny Masterson has lost the appeal of his rape conviction, meaning his 30-year prison sentence has been upheld.

The actor, best known for his role on That ’70s Show, was convicted in 2023 of two counts of rape against two women in 2003, while a third charge relating to a third plaintiff, who alleged she was raped by Masterson in 2001, was quashed.

Masterson has insisted that sex with all three plaintiffs was consensual. In December he filed an appeal, questioning the plaintiffs’ credibility and claiming he didn’t receive a fair trial as the judge, Los Angeles superior court judge Charlaine F Olmedo, was biased against Scientology.

In an 89-page ruling filed in the California court of appeal on Tuesday, a three-judge panel rejected Masterson’s arguments, finding that Olmedo’s statements during the trial showed “no animus or departure from neutrality regarding Scientology”.

During the trial, prosecutors argued that Masterson, a prominent Scientologist, had used his role in the church – of which all three plaintiffs were also members at the time – to avoid accountability for the assaults. Prosecutors also argued the plaintiffs had delayed reporting the incidents due to their fear they would violate a Scientology rule against going to the police and be retaliated against.

Two of his accusers testified that when they reported Masterson to Scientology officials, they were told they were not raped, were put through “ethics programs” which they likened to repeated interrogations, and were warned against going to police. One of the women said she was shunned and ostracised for doing so.

Olmedo allowed a former Scientologist, Claire Headley, to testify as an expert about the church’s beliefs and practices. Headley told the court that Scientology regards going to law enforcement as a “suppressive act” that was sanctionable by excommunication.
In his appeal, Masterson’s lawyers argued the court had improperly intruded into interpretation of church doctrine.

“The jury in this case was not asked to determine the truth or falsity of Scientology doctrine or beliefs,” the appeals court panel wrote. “Admission of Scientology evidence for those purposes did not contravene the First Amendment.”
The panel also rejected separate arguments about the statute of limitations and evidentiary rulings, and denied that he did not get an adequate defense.
Masterson’s lawyers, Cliff Gardner and Eric Multhaup, called it an “unfortunate decision”, telling Variety they would appeal to the California supreme court.
After Masterson was found guilty in 2023, the church of Scientology issued a statement to say the “testimony and descriptions of Scientology beliefs” during the trial were “uniformly false”.
“The church has no policy prohibiting or discouraging members from reporting criminal conduct of anyone – Scientologists or not – to law enforcement,” the statement said.

items: Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. articles.title: King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit
articles.summary:
Royal tour of Caribbean comes as Commonwealth nations renew calls for Britain to engage in reparation talks

King Charles has confirmed that he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit…

blocks.text: King Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit with Commonwealth leaders as he begins his Caribbean tour.
The king arrived in the Bahamas to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973.
His visit comes amid renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for the atrocities of transatlantic slavery and engage in reparations talks.
Charles’s nine-day tour, which includes a solo state visit to Guyana, will culminate in presiding over the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) hosted by Antigua and Barbuda.
In his speech in the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles said: “Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness.

“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future.”
He said the Chogm leaders would discuss matters relating to the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua.
But a statement from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee said the king’s comments on Tuesday “fall short of what justice requires”.

“Our culture is not born out of darkness; our culture was born out of agency and out of the will to survive despite the horrors, trauma and degradation. Our culture is a testament to the power of the human spirit, not simply a reaction to the worst examples of it.
“We therefore do not need King Charles to tell us how outstanding our culture is … We need him to speak about his role in the darkness and how he plans to atone for it actively.

“The royal family and the British government were responsible for the darkness. His comments fall short of what justice requires – a full and formal apology – and they do not speak to the steps needed to remedy the wrongs committed in the name of the crown he wears.”

Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, told the Guardian that while she appreciated the king’s attempt to “connect with Bahamian culture” in his speech his words felt “like hollow platitudes”.

She added: “I am very proud of my Bahamian people and the beautiful spirit and hospitality that they shared. My critique is not an attempt to rain on their parade. It is because of this pride that I feel we deserve so much more than what was offered.”
The chair of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Prof Hilary Beckles, said what the Caribbean was looking for was “proprietary justice, beginning with remorse”.

Beckles added that when speaking to Caribbean young people the king should “dig deep within his consciousness” and give to them “the empowerment that he would give to his own children” to survive in a rapidly changing world. Anything short of that would be to condone and minimise the legacy of harm and suffering that continues today, he said.
Charles is to travel to Guyana on Thursday where the president, Mohamed Irfaan Ali, recently called for the monarch to take the next step and offer to apologise.
The king follows the guidance of his ministers, and it is understood the government has not advised him to offer an apology or reparations, in keeping with established policy.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will join Charles in Antigua for the gathering of Commonwealth leaders.

Charles acknowledged the “appalling atrocity of slavery”, describing it as something “which forever stains our history, when he attended the ceremony marking Barbados’s historic transition to a republic in 2021.

A year later he described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to “deepen my own understanding of slavery’s enduring impact”, in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “At the request of host governments, the king’s programme will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future that are having a transformative effect on the region, as it confronts the challenges of today.

“For his majesty, this tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past. This will therefore also be reflected in differing ways and words during the tour, as you would expect.”
Additional reporting by Press Association

articles.title: Experts urge 'global health emergency' as climate harms accelerate
articles.summary: Heat, drought and storms linked to climate change are already killing millions worldwide. Researchers want global warming to be declared a global health emergency as the health harms from it escalate…

image.caption: A heatstroke patient is treated in Chennai, India. Climate change caused more than half a million heat deaths in 2023 aloneImage: Pugazh Murugan/ Matrix Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: As heat deaths, drought and food insecurity accelerate worldwide, nearly 150 researchers from more than 30 countries are calling for climate change to be declared a "global health emergency."

The health and economic toll of planetary heating has risen sharply in the decade since countries signed the Paris climate accord — a landmark deal to stop climate change that was hailed by the World Health Organization (WHO) at the time as "the most important public health agreement of the century."

Yet, climate change was responsible for more than half a million heat deaths in 2023 alone and nearly 3 million since 2016. The area affected by extreme drought, which threatens food and water supplies and raises the risk of disease, grew more than 700% faster than in the decade before. And heat cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost potential income last year, all according to the annual Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change.

"This cannot continue," said Alan Dangour, director of climate and health at Wellcome Trust, one of the world's largest charities, which funded the Lancet report. "We must change course and put the health and well-being of people at the heart of our response to climate change — measuring success not through emissions targets or degrees Celsius but by lives saved and health outcomes improved."
Climate extremes are the new health threats — here is why
Climate-linked health harms growing faster than before
The latest findings from the Lancet study show how rapidly the health risks are growing by comparing this decade to the one before the Paris Agreement was signed.

Heat is the starkest example. Climate change was responsible for 68% of heat-related deaths between 2016 and 2023, up from 55% in the previous decade. The yearly increase in climate-driven heat deaths more than doubled over the same period.

But deaths are only "the tip of the iceberg," said Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney's Heat and Health Research Center. "Except that iceberg is not melting, it's growing every year." Beneath the surface are also heatstroke, lost sleep, and worsening chronic health conditions.

blocks.caption: Older people are particularly vulnerable to extreme heat Image: Rolf Vennenbernd/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The economic harms are mounting too. Working in extreme heat puts people at risk of heat exhaustion, illness or injury and, ultimately, losing income and livelihoods.

Heat wiped out 573 billion potential working hours in 2025, with farmworkers bearing the brunt. Vulnerable economies in Africa and South-East Asia were hit hardest with losses reaching 5% of GDP, compared with 0.5% in the more developed economies.

"The economic toll is battering vulnerable sectors and communities the hardest," Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown, who is based at University College London, told journalists at a press briefing.

Water extremes are intensifying too. Satellite data show that since 2003, 43% of the world's land has been steadily drying out, while 37% has been getting wetter. Together, that is more than 80% of land shifting to extremes that threaten crops, food supplies, and sanitation.
Why Europe's extreme summers are getting worse
Drought can leave people without safe drinking water and raises the risk of infectious disease, while floods bring drowning, injury and contaminated water.
Heat waves and droughts pushed nearly 128 million more people into food insecurity in 2024, compared with the 1981–2010 average.
"This isn't a gradual worsening; it's a step change," Romanello said.
What would declaring a global health emergency change?

To save lives and protect human health, experts are calling for a new WHO instrument to help countries share information, coordinate responses, monitor threats, and disburse funds. The United Nations and its member states would create the mechanism.

The closest existing version of this is the WHO's Public Health Emergency of International Concern mechanism (PHEIC) used during the COVID-19 pandemic and mpox outbreaks. But built with short-term emergencies in mind, it falls short of addressing a complex threat that requires sustained global action across multiple sectors, like climate change.

The world needs a broader approach, "so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency," said Romanello. "We're doing a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies."
Progress happening but not nearly fast enough

Romanello told journalists that "we have more than enough proof" that such action does improve health outcomes. "Early warning systems informed by climate, have already seen a reduction in the adverse impacts of these extreme weather events," she said.
The growth in renewable energy has also partly aided a reduction in deaths from fossil fuel air pollution in half of 140 countries assessed since 2016, preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.
And 56 countries now have national plans to adapt their health services for climate impacts, such as heat waves and disease outbreaks, up from just 14 in 2015.

blocks.caption: An increase in renewable energy and other climate actions have helped reduce air pollution in some countries. But not everywhere Image: Muda Sagala/AFP

blocks.text: But progress remains too slow, according to the report.
Fossil fuels, the burning of which releases emissions fueling planetary heating as well as other pollutants, still supply more than 80% of the world's energy.

Energy-related emissions hit a record high in 2024. The world's 100 largest oil and gas companies are on track to produce 150% more oil and gas by 2040 than is compatible with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit). A year ago, that figure was 138%.
Investing in an old technology
Governments continue to fund fossil fuels, with net subsidies doubling since 2016 to $6.2 trillion. In 2024, 10 countries spent more on such subsidies than on their entire health systems.
Yet as fossil fuel prices rise and renewables become cheaper, these polluting technologies are becoming increasingly uneconomical, said Romanello.

Romanello likened new fossil fuel investment to "investing in Blockbuster when you have Netflix," — a bet on an old technology, referring to the once ubiquitous video rental store that failed to adapt to streaming.

Meanwhile, money to help health systems adapt to climate change is scarce. Developing countries estimate they need around $3.3 billion a year for such adaptations, which the Lancet authors say is likely an underestimate. Only about a third of that was committed in 2024. Foreign aid reductions, led by the US and followed by Germany, which made the second-largest cut, are widening the gap.

"This report is a stark warning that climate change is a health emergency," said Helen Clark, former prime minister of New Zealand and chair of the Lancet Countdown's board. "What's missing is not evidence, but the political will to act on it."
